proofs.why: dropping Table S row S1 from the accepted-cut predicate makes EVERY buffer position a candidate cut instead of only the positions immediately after a newline, so the transform stops buffering to a line boundary and emits whatever it holds. A labelled credential whose two halves arrive in separate pushes is then scanned as two separate regions, neither of which matches the rule on its own, and the complete key lands in the durable log byte-for-byte — the WD-SINK-CHUNK leak this package's region contract exists to close.

proofs.why: dropping Table S row S2 lets the predicate cut at a newline that still has a sensitive key binder open — `password:` with its value yet to arrive, the same shape with a blank line between, the keyword and its separator on separate lines, and the CRLF form of the second. Each of the four is redacted when scanned whole (the legacy assignment rule's separator group is `\s*`, which spans line breaks) and each leaks across a cut a last-line-only predicate permits, which is exactly the round-1 design finding this row encodes.

proofs.why: dropping Table S row S3 lets the predicate cut inside a quoted JSON value that is still open. The structured-JSON rule's value body excludes only the quote and the backslash, so it INCLUDES the newline and the value stays open across arbitrarily many lines; cutting at the first of those newlines splits the rule and neither region matches, so the value reaches the log unredacted.

That rule's body spans arbitrarily many lines by construction, so a block whose opener and closer arrive in different pushes is split into regions in which neither half matches, and the key body lands in the durable log in full.
